Cardiology and hematology · published research

Hypertension

A 2025 meta-analysis reported lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure across sustained PBM protocols, but certainty was very low and results varied widely. Short-term physiological findings are favorable in selected settings, while sustained control in diagnosed hypertension remains unproven.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

PBM may lower blood pressure in some sustained and acute protocols, but the clinical evidence is heterogeneous and at high risk of bias. Findings do not yet establish durable control in people with diagnosed hypertension.

Summary of the Evidence

Clinical findings are mixed. A 2025 meta-analysis of sustained protocols reported lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure, but certainty was very low and results varied widely. A small healthy-volunteer crossover found a short-term systolic response, while a post-mastectomy randomized trial found no between-group blood-pressure difference. Several rat models reported lower pressure, but sustained control in diagnosed hypertension remains unproven.

Human and clinical evidence

A 2025 meta-analysis pooled three randomized trials with 169 participants. Compared with control, sham, or antihypertensive therapy, the pooled mean difference was −15.87 mmHg for systolic pressure and −8.73 mmHg for diastolic pressure. Confidence intervals excluded no difference, but heterogeneity was considerable and the review rated certainty very low because the trials had high risk of bias (Espósito et al. 2025).

A randomized study of 27 women treated after mastectomy and taking hormone blockers found no significant between-group difference in systolic or diastolic pressure, although heart rate fell in the treatment group (Pacheco et al. 2024). A separate randomized crossover experiment in 14 healthy adults found that whole-body visible blue-light exposure lowered systolic pressure and improved arterial-stiffness and endothelial measures. This was a short-term physiological experiment, not a treatment trial for diagnosed hypertension (Stern et al. 2018).

Animal evidence

Seven rat publications used models including spontaneous, renovascular, diet-associated, or hormone-related hypertension. Several reported lower blood pressure after red-light treatment, though not all animals responded equally. A dose-comparison experiment found a larger response at an intermediate energy and no hypotensive response at the highest tested exposure. A longer study in high-fat-diet rats reported prevention of a blood-pressure rise alongside changes in nitric oxide and endothelial function (Oishi et al. 2024).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

One rat publication also included laboratory work on vasodilation and nitric-oxide-related mechanisms. This is part of that animal publication, not a separate hypertension trial.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human protocols are not interchangeable. The post-mastectomy study used 660-nm visible red light near the carotid artery for 15 minutes across 16 sessions over four weeks. The paper and database differ on the reported energy per session, so that value is omitted here. The healthy-volunteer experiment used 450-nm visible blue light over the body for 30 minutes. Sustained-protocol trials in the meta-analysis also used different comparators and delivery approaches. Rat studies most often used 660-nm red light, with some 780- or 830-nm near-infrared light.

Interpretation

Pooled sustained-protocol estimates favor PBM for systolic and diastolic pressure, but certainty is very low and results vary widely between trials. Acute physiological findings and several rat studies are favorable in selected settings, while one randomized post-mastectomy study found no between-group blood-pressure difference. Durable benefit in diagnosed hypertension has not been demonstrated.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Sustained-protocol meta-analysis: systolic blood pressure mean difference −15.87 mmHg (95% CI −27.11 to −4.64; I²=92%).

Diastolic blood pressure mean difference −8.73 mmHg (95% CI −15.19 to −2.26; I²=94%), based on three randomized trials with 169 participants (Espósito et al. 2025).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for sustained blood-pressure control in diagnosed hypertension.

Low for short-term blood-pressure changes in selected light-exposure settings.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The pooled sustained-protocol estimates favor PBM, but the contributing randomized trials had high risk of bias, comparators and protocols differed, and results varied widely. The healthy-volunteer crossover supports only an acute physiological effect, while the post-mastectomy trial found no between-group blood-pressure difference. Sustained benefit in diagnosed hypertension remains uncertain (Espósito et al. 2025).
